mainEntity.name: What is the difference between mutually exclusive and independent events?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A ∩ B) = 0. Independent events can happen together, and one occurring does not change the probability of the other, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). If both have non-zero probability, events cannot be both.

mainEntity.name: Why can’t I just add probabilities for “A or B”?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the events can overlap, adding counts the overlap twice. The addition rule subtracts P(A ∩ B) once to correct this. Adding alone is only right for mutually exclusive events.

It updates a prior probability when you observe new evidence. It reverses a conditional probability: from P(B | A), how likely the evidence is if A is true, to P(A | B), how likely A is given the evidence, taking into account how common A was to begin with.
It is the mistaken belief that past independent outcomes change future ones — for example that heads is “due” after a run of tails. For independent events, P(A | B) = P(A): the coin has no memory.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert probability to odds?

acceptedAnswer.text: Odds in favour are p ÷ (1 − p). A probability of 0.4 gives odds of 0.4 ÷ 0.6 = 2 to 3 in favour, or 3 to 2 against. Use the Odds tab to convert in either direction.

mainEntity.name: Can a probability be greater than 1 or negative?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Every probability lies between 0 and 1 inclusive (0% to 100%). The calculator rejects values outside that range, and joint probabilities that are impossible given P(A) and P(B).
